clue.text: Head-in-air Athenian architect

parts.note: the legendary craftsman of Athens who built the Labyrinth and flew on wings of wax and feathers, so his head was literally in the air

explanation.surface: A dreamy, absent-minded Athenian designer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head-in-air' looks like a jibe about absent-mindedness, but it points to the myth of the inventor who escaped Crete by flying.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this Athenian inventor designed the Cretan Labyrinth and flew away on home-made wings.

clue.text: Day came, unusually for seat of learning

indicators.note: something done unusually is done out of the normal order, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A day dawned, against habit, for a centre of study.
explanation.definitionFit: A school or college for advanced study is a seat of learning, the phrase for any such institution.

clue.text: Sister of Meleager, whose husband displayed a fatal need to change his shirt

definitions.text: Sister of Meleager, whose husband displayed a fatal need to change his shirt

parts.words: Sister of Meleager, whose husband displayed a fatal need to change his shirt
parts.note: the wife of Heracles, who sent him a shirt soaked in the centaur Nessus's poisoned blood; it burned him so badly he tore at it and died

explanation.surface: A mythical woman whose husband desperately needed a fresh shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: The shirt of Nessus clung to Heracles and burned him, so his 'need to change his shirt' was literal and fatal.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth she was Meleager's sister and the wife of Heracles, whom she killed unknowingly with the poisoned shirt.

clue.text: It was visited by Paul as part of wily strategy

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A place the apostle came to, as a piece of cunning planning.
explanation.definitionFit: Acts records that the apostle preached and was stoned at this town in Lycaonia during his missionary journeys.

clue.text: A basket case, thrashed by possessive husband, pinched and punched by fairies

definitions.text: A basket case, thrashed by possessive husband, pinched and punched by fairies

parts.words: A basket case, thrashed by possessive husband, pinched and punched by fairies
parts.note: in The Merry Wives of Windsor the fat knight is carried out in a laundry basket, beaten by the jealous Ford, and pinched by children dressed as fairies

explanation.surface: A hopeless wreck, beaten by a jealous husband and tormented by fairies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Basket case' reads as slang for a hopeless person, but the knight was literally carried off in a basket of dirty washing.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's fat knight suffers each of these humiliations in The Merry Wives of Windsor.

clue.text: Kept in suspense for punishment

parts.note: read literally, being left suspended from a rope as a penalty describes execution on the gallows

explanation.surface: Someone left waiting anxiously as a penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kept in suspense' suggests anxious waiting, but read literally it means hung from a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Executed on the gallows, the past participle used for capital punishment by rope.

clue.text: Demigoddess, portrayed in half articles

parts.note: hemi- is the Greek prefix for half
the is the definite article
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A minor goddess depicted in half the articles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'articles' gives both THE and A, the two English articles; 'portrayed in' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend she was a mortal princess of Tenedos who was worshipped as a minor goddess after death.

clue.text: Lewis observed one who did

parts.note: C. S. Lewis wrote A Grief Observed after his wife died, so he watched himself mourning

explanation.surface: Lewis watched someone who acted.
explanation.walkthrough: The title A Grief Observed lies behind 'Lewis observed': Lewis observed his own grief, being one who mourned.
explanation.definitionFit: Felt sorrow for a loss, as Lewis did after his wife's death.

clue.text: A quarrelsome pair, of Fry's angels perhaps

definitions.text: A quarrelsome pair, of Fry's angels perhaps

parts.words: A quarrelsome pair, of Fry's angels perhaps
parts.note: two people who settle a quarrel with swords or pistols, here linked to a scene of fighting in a Christopher Fry play

explanation.surface: Two argumentative figures, perhaps from a playwright's angels.
explanation.definitionFit: Two combatants in a formal fight over a point of honour make a quarrelsome pair.

clue.text: Crowne'd king

parts.note: John Crowne wrote the tragedy ..., King of Persia, so the king belongs to Crowne as well as wearing a crown

explanation.surface: A monarch who has had his coronation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crowne'd' looks like an old spelling of crowned, but it is the possessive of the Restoration dramatist John Crowne.
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian monarch is the title figure of John Crowne's 1688 tragedy.

clue.text: More Nazi version to render in the Latin alphabet

indicators.note: a new version of something is a reworking, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A more fascist edition, translated into Roman script.
explanation.definitionFit: To transliterate a script such as Cyrillic into Roman letters.

clue.text: Swiss city road mistaken by Hamlet character

parts.note: Bern is the Swiss capital

indicators.note: something mistaken has gone wrong, so the letters of the word are muddled

explanation.surface: A Swiss road taken wrongly by someone from Hamlet.
explanation.definitionFit: He is one of the officers on watch who see the Ghost in the opening scene of the play.

clue.text: Journey of composer from junction

indicators.note: the composer comes from the junction, so his name follows the letter

parts.note: a T-junction, so T stands for a junction
Maurice Ravel, the French composer

explanation.surface: A composer's journey from a road junction.
explanation.definitionFit: To go on a trip, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Semi-legendary kingdom in enemy Siam

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the clue's next words, across the gap between them

explanation.surface: An ancient realm inside Thailand's old foe.
explanation.definitionFit: A region of north-west Asia Minor that appears in Homer and early legend as a realm.

clue.text: Loch seems rough for Czech composer

indicators.note: rough water is churned up, so the letters of the words are thrown about

explanation.surface: A Scottish lake looks choppy to a composer from Prague.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignaz Moscheles, Prague-born pianist and composer, friend and teacher of Mendelssohn.

clue.text: Giant Spanish novelist in the end American

indicators.note: the novelist is placed in the end, split around his name

parts.note: the end is simply the word end
Camilo José Cela, the Spanish Nobel laureate

explanation.surface: A huge Spanish writer, ultimately American.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth he was one of the giants who fought the gods, buried under Etna.

clue.text: Gerald Seymour's highflyer

parts.note: Gerald Seymour wrote a thriller with this title, and an angel of the top rank flies high

explanation.surface: A rising star in a thriller writer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Highflyer' suggests an ambitious person, but it is a winged heavenly being, which is also the title of Seymour's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A chief angel, a heavenly being of the highest order, and the title of a Gerald Seymour thriller.

clue.text: Novelist identified by her weight

parts.note: by in the sense 'at' a place, as in 'by the door'
taken as written
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A writer known by how heavy she is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'identified' only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Gertrude Atherton was an American writer of popular novels about California.

clue.text: Waugh character, twice wrecked in Shakespeare

explanation.surface: A Waugh figure shipwrecked two times in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Sebastian Flyte is in Brideshead Revisited; Shakespeare's two men of that name are shipwrecked in Twelfth Night and The Tempest.

clue.text: Price adoptive daughter of this park lady

definitions.text: Price adoptive daughter of this park lady

parts.words: Price adoptive daughter of this park lady
parts.note: in Mansfield Park Fanny Price is brought up by her aunt, the lady of the house at Mansfield

explanation.surface: Someone adopted as a daughter by a lady from a park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Price' looks like a cost, but it is Fanny Price, Jane Austen's heroine of Mansfield Park.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Bertram of Mansfield Park takes in her niece Fanny Price and raises her.

clue.text: Sea-god in wrecked canoe (American)

indicators.note: a wrecked boat is smashed up, so the letters of the word are broken and rearranged

explanation.surface: A god of the sea in a smashed American canoe.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Titan who personified the great river encircling the world.

clue.text: Its great woman prophetically bore a son, who lived and died and lived again

definitions.text: Its great woman prophetically bore a son, who lived and died and lived again

parts.words: Its great woman prophetically bore a son, who lived and died and lived again
parts.note: in 2 Kings 4 a wealthy woman of this town is promised a son by Elisha; the boy later dies and the prophet revives him

explanation.surface: A place whose leading woman had a son as foretold, who died and rose again.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical town of the Shunammite woman whose son Elisha foretold and raised from the dead.

clue.text: Hardly Corneille's Life of Walpole

parts.note: Corneille wrote a tragedy with this title, and Walpole's first name was the same, but the play is not about him

explanation.surface: A French dramatist's play that is not quite a biography of Walpole.
explanation.walkthrough: Corneille's tragedy is about the Roman champion who fought the Curiatii; it shares only a name with Horace Walpole, so it is 'hardly' his life.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Corneille's 1640 tragedy and the first name of the writer Walpole.

clue.text: Pianist blanches in new composition

indicators.note: a new composition puts the same material into a fresh arrangement, so the letters of the word are reordered

explanation.surface: A pianist goes pale at an unfamiliar piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Artur Schnabel, the Austrian concert pianist famous for his Beethoven recordings.

clue.text: Mother of fathers of Rome

parts.note: Acca, the foster-mother of the twins who founded Rome, was also mother of the twelve Arval Brothers, a priesthood called fathers

explanation.surface: The mother of Rome's founders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fathers of Rome' points to Romulus and Remus, its founding fathers, whom she nursed.
explanation.definitionFit: Acca, the Roman woman who in legend nursed Romulus and Remus.

clue.text: O Casey gave him the Needle "

definitions.text: O Casey gave him the Needle

parts.words: O Casey gave him the Needle
parts.note: Sean O'Casey named a character Needle, giving him the nickname as a playwright gives a character a name

explanation.surface: The playwright annoyed someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gave him the Needle' sounds like teasing, but O'Casey gave a character the nickname Needle.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of O'Casey's character nicknamed Needle.

clue.text: Polesitter not new for him in Belgian novelist

indicators.note: not says a letter is missing from the novelist's name

parts.note: Georges Simenon, the Belgian creator of Maigret

explanation.surface: A man on a pole, not new, inside a Belgian writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Saint Simeon Stylites lived for decades on top of a pillar, hence 'Polesitter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Simeon Stylites spent thirty-seven years living on a pillar.

clue.text: "If you come to live in our house, and be a — amongst us" (Thomas Heywood, The Wise Woman of Hogsdon)

definitions.text: "If you come to live in our house, and be a — amongst us" (Thomas Heywood, The Wise Woman of Hogsdon)

parts.words: "If you come to live in our house, and be a — amongst us" (Thomas Heywood, The Wise Woman of Hogsdon)
parts.note: the missing word in Heywood's line names a member of a household religious sect
